title: The Solver and the Atlas: finding a formula, crossing a stability limit, reading a phase plane and a saddle
summary: Four screenshots of the Solver and Atlas workspaces: symbolic regression picks a formula from a Pareto front of complexity against loss; the heat equation is run just beyond its stability limit; the phase plane of a harmonic oscillator shows a centre; and a saddle surface is shown in 2D contours and in 3D.

media.alt: Screenshot of the Solver, PDE tab. Left, the controls for the heat equation with a hat-shaped initial profile and a ratio r equal to 0.52, described as past the stability cliff. Centre, a zigzag of vertical teal lines across the plot, the finite-difference solution at the final time, which should be a gentle dashed arch. Right, a space-time image in red and blue with a noisy upper edge. Top right, a readout states r equals 0.520 UNSTABLE and a maximum difference from the exact series of 2.85e+09.

read_the_figure.question: Is the numerical solution trustworthy, and what in the figure tells me so?
read_the_figure.axes: PDE: position along the rod (horizontal) against temperature (vertical) at the final time, with a dashed yellow exact series; right, space-time map. Phase plane: x (horizontal) against y (vertical) with arrows. Regression: data and fit, a Pareto plot of complexity (horizontal) against loss (vertical), and a table of candidate formulas. Saddle: x and y contours and a 3D surface.
look_at: The heat solution: the exact series (the dashed yellow arch) is the reference; the teal zigzag is the unstable finite-difference solution, and the printed maximum difference from the series is 2.85e+09. Any non-smooth, huge oscillation is a numerical instability, not physics.
The readout says r = 0.520 and UNSTABLE. The stability limit for this scheme is r <= 1/2: the ratio of time step to the square of the space step.
Phase plane: arrows rotate around the origin; the readout lists the equilibrium (0, 0) as a centre (linearly) with trace 0 and determinant 1.

Symbolic regression: the Pareto plot drops steeply and then flattens; the table lists candidate formulas with complexity, loss and a 'score' (the biggest drop in log loss per unit complexity); the selected formula is the elbow, here complexity 5 with a loss of order 1e-11.
Saddle: contours of z = x^2 - y^2 form an X; the 3D surface curves up along one axis and down along the other; an arrow shows the gradient at a point.
read_the_figure.proves: For the heat equation the printed ratio r and the error against an exact series show that the scheme fails past r = 1/2 regardless of the grid fineness. The regression table shows how a formula is chosen from a set of equally plausible ones. The phase plane and the saddle illustrate the classification of equilibria by the sign of curvature or eigenvalues.
if_wrong: A smooth profile that nonetheless disagrees by a large factor with the exact series: check r first.
An r above 0.5 labelled stable: wrong limit for this scheme.
Picking the lowest-loss formula in the table: it is the most complex and probably overfitted.
An equilibrium labelled centre from a linearization with zero trace: borderline; nonlinear terms decide.
must_check: That the stability parameter and its limit are both printed.
That the numerical solution is compared with an exact one at the same time.
That the regression selection rule is stated, not only the best loss.
That the equilibrium's trace and determinant are printed.

terms.meaning: Forward time, centred space: explicit finite differences for the heat equation.
The ratio of the time step to the square of the space step times the diffusivity.
The set of formulas not beaten in both complexity and loss.
An equilibrium of a planar system with purely imaginary eigenvalues: closed orbits.
A critical point where the Hessian has one positive and one negative eigenvalue.

remember: FTCS for the heat equation is stable only for r <= 1/2.
A mode of wavelength 2 Delta x is amplified fastest and sets the limit.
The best formula is the knee of the Pareto front, not its lowest-loss end.
A planar linear system is a centre when trace = 0 and determinant > 0.
A saddle of z = x^2 - y^2 has Hessian diag(2, -2).

steps.title: von Neumann stability of FTCS
steps.note: The worst mode has sin^2 equal to 1, so G = 1 - 4r; at r = 0.52 this is -1.08, magnitude above one, with alternating sign: the zigzag of the picture.

steps.title: What 1.08 per step does
steps.note: If a unit-amplitude zigzag mode grows at this rate, about 283 steps produce an error of 2.85e9, the printed value. This is an estimate under that assumption, not a statement about the code.

steps.title: Phase plane of the oscillator
steps.note: A centre. Orbits are circles of constant H; the printed trace 0 and determinant 1 are the matrix's.

steps.title: Gradient and Hessian of the saddle
steps.note: Mixed-sign eigenvalues of the Hessian make a saddle. The arrow on the contour plot is the gradient at a point; it is perpendicular to the contour.

worked.title: Amplification of the worst mode
worked.problem: For r = 0.52 and r = 0.48, find the amplification factor of the 2 Delta x mode and its size after 100 steps.
worked.answer: Growth by a factor 2200 against decay by 4e-4 after 100 steps: a 4 percent change in r flips the behaviour.

analyze.q: Why does the stability limit depend on r and not on the time step alone?
analyze.hint: Time step against the square of the space step.

checks.q: What does r = 0.52 mean in the heat screenshot?
checks.answer: The time step is 0.52 of the largest stable multiple of the squared space step: just past r = 1/2.

checks.q: Why does the solution alternate in sign from cell to cell?
checks.answer: The most amplified mode has G < -1, so its sign flips every step and every cell, producing a zigzag.

checks.q: If the error against the exact series is 1e-3, is the scheme stable?
checks.answer: Not necessarily: a mode with |G| just above 1 grows slowly, so a short run can still look accurate; the r value is the reliable test.

checks.q: Propose an implicit alternative and say what happens to the stability limit.
checks.answer: Backward time, centred space: G = 1/(1 + 4 r sin^2(k dx/2)), always below one: stable for any r, at the price of solving a linear system each step.
